reviewerOveralls.codex: The accepted view is not fieldable as written, though it is substantially clearer than the committed view and most of the 33 suggestions are faithful simplifications, with the numerical bonus examples and cross-tab dollar amounts mostly reconciling. Three critical blockers must be resolved before launch: the untruthful description of the transformed 10-90 endorsement-strength display, the absence of any tie outcome/payment rule, and the Vertex/Atlas organization mismatch between tabs. Beyond those, there are major construct-validity issues (mandated public backing is costly organizational endorsement, not complete sponsorship; strength and wager each conflate multiple motives), a color-confounded gender manipulation, a missing evaluator-gender item, unresolved outcome-sequence cells/power/stream supply, and unverifiable rendered screens and links. The comprehension checks are answerable from the participant-facing text with one defensible marked answer each, and the payment mechanics reconcile except for the named exceptions. Final acceptance decision on the 33 suggestions: reject 0, 3, and 19; amend 7, 20, 24, 28, 31, and 32; accept all others as faithful simplifications.
reviewerOveralls.construct: The accepted view is close to fieldable and is a real construct upgrade over the OLD paradigm: must-endorse plus org assignment converts a two-sided forecast into compelled public advocacy (direction is uninformative by design and CQ3 makes that common knowledge, so all signal lives in strength), the three-part bonus gives the sponsor genuine skin in the game, and the wager-plus-allocation package makes the audience consequential to the sponsor, which is the core of sponsorship as distinct from cheap talk. The org match is doing real work, not decoration: it naturalizes must-endorse, licenses evaluator discounting of inflated strength, and carries the org-level DV. Three construct gaps need attention before fielding: (1) the sponsorship tie is categorical (org) rather than dyadic — the endorser backs a new candidate every round, so frame claims as organizational sponsorship/advocacy, not sponsor-protege relationships; (2) the allocation DVs are costless transfers labeled "future review slots" with no review mechanism behind them, which both violates the literal-truth constraint and leaves gender-differential generosity as a rival explanation; (3) gender carried only by avatar hue risks low manipulation-check pass rates and a selected passers subsample. The exit self-endorsement item is ill-posed as written (no defined comparison event) and needs a one-sentence fix. Of the 33 suggestions, none are fatal for the sponsorship construct; I would amend suggestions 3 and 23 (minor agency/sincerity wording) and accept the rest from a construct standpoint.
reviewerOveralls.comprehension: On clarity grounds the accepted view is fieldable after small patches: it is genuinely easier to read than the committed text (shorter sentences, concrete formulas, and the "in total" edits to endorser CQ1 options — ids 10-13 — fix a real ambiguity), and every comprehension check (2 endorser, 7 evaluator) is answerable from the instruction text alone with exactly one defensible keyed answer, each taught before the check appears. No suggestion needs outright rejection for clarity, but four should be amended rather than accepted as-is: id 0 (restore "assigned to represent" — its loss both weakens the sponsorship framing on the endorser side and orphans the "represent" vocabulary in CQ2's keyed answer), id 24 (the evaluator is never told the strength scale, which the wager DV depends on), id 17 (org-equals-candidate category error), and ids 18/25/32 (three 32-39-word sentences to split). The two clarity problems that most threaten the design are not in the 33 suggestions at all: allocation item 1's "allocate to seeing more endorsements" plants a belief the study does not deliver (against the project's own truthfulness note, on the focal social-capital DV), and the exit self-endorsement item is unparseable as written. Sponsorship-wise, the accepted instructions still convey own-org backing with skin in the game, but the dropped assignment language and the dropped "putting your money where your mouth is" signaling clause slightly thin the sponsor-role framing on the endorser side; the one-clause fix to id 0 recovers most of it.
reviewerOveralls.mechanics: All dollar figures and formulas check out: the endorser 3-part bonus ($1+$1+$1=$3), every CQ1 worked example in the design note ($0.50/$0.50/$1.80-unique-max/$0.75), the evaluator wager arithmetic ($0.55/$0.45 example, $0.75 CQ key, 3x$1.00=$3.00 cap), and the slot math (20x$0.05=$1.00) are internally correct and consistent across the two tabs; none of the 33 suggestions introduces a numeric error, and several (10-13, 27, 31, 32) improve precision or truthfulness. The mechanics-side blockers are truthfulness gaps rather than arithmetic: the payment mapping is undefined if the randomly picked endorsement has no reviewer (and the accepted view's categorical "Evaluators review your endorsements. For each one, they see..." is not guaranteed true under cell-sampling); both tabs tell participants evaluators see "the endorsement strength they set" while the implementation shows a 10-90 remapped value; and the "future review slots" label promises a future-review mechanism the design notes explicitly decline to implement. On incentive compatibility, the allocation DV has zero opportunity cost (allocating all slots is weakly dominant for any non-spiteful evaluator, so expect ceiling), and the linear wager/strength payoffs are not proper scoring rules, with component 2 giving endorsers a strength-inflation motive that makes the evaluator-tab sentence "strength showed how confident they were" an overstatement. The accepted view is fieldable on mechanics once the reviewed-endorsement coverage guarantee, the strength-display wording, and the future-review label are resolved; I would amend suggestions 4/5 (restore a "for each endorsement they review"-type qualifier), 25/26 (past tense for realized outcomes), and 9 (allocated vs possible slots), and accept the rest.
reviewerOveralls.fidelity: The accepted view is a faithful compression of the committed redesign: 29 of 33 suggestions are pure compression or outright improvements — several add precision rather than losing it (2 and 7 add "in that set"; 10-13 add "in total," keeping CQ1's unique-max payout structure intact; 28-30 add the explicit dollar-wager conversion that supports CQ5; 31 fixes tense to the literally true past; 32 adds the $0.05/slot and $1.00-cap details so the two tabs now state identical allocation mechanics; 27 fixes the untrue plural "your wagers"). The meaningful deviations are concentrated in two Endorser-tab suggestions: 8 (drops "The more they trust your endorsement, the more you earn") and 18 (drops "putting your money where your mouth is," "signals weaker backing," and the "when you are unsure" calibration cue) — together these strip the public-backing/audience-signaling frame from the sponsor's incentive text, so both should be amended before acceptance, not accepted as-is. Relative to the OLD baseline, all real deviation comes from the redesign itself (must-endorse, org affiliation, $0.50 bank, three-part bonus), which was already committed; this simplification pass adds no further drift and preserves the OLD text's surviving elements (subset not in chronological order, wager on correctness, endorser pay depends on both accuracy and your wager). Safe to accept as-is: 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 16, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32, plus 15 and 17 accepted strictly as a pair, and 24 accepted with a follow-up to sync the live survey's "Endorser's confidence" label. Amend before accepting: 8 and 18. Optional light amendments: 0 (restore "assigned"), 3 (restore person-level referent); 25 is fine as-is and its dropped "well-calibrated" should stay dropped on truthfulness grounds. With 8 and 18 amended, the accepted view is fieldable and recognizably close to both the committed design text and the original paradigm.

mergeNote: The five reviewers converged strongly on a small core: the unimplemented "future review slots" telegraph and the Vertex/Atlas placeholder were each flagged by four reviewers, while ties, the 10-90 display remap, gender carried only by avatar color, the costless allocation DV, the ill-posed self-endorsement exit item, the strength-equals-confidence sentence, and the dropped assignment framing each drew two to three independent flags — so 61 raw findings merged to 41 distinct issues. The remainder were single-reviewer findings that split cleanly by lens (mechanics gaps, comprehension stalls, suggestion-fidelity drift, construct validity) with essentially no contradictions; the only mild tension is fidelity wanting suggestion 18's dropped signaling clauses restored while comprehension wants that same sentence shortened, which a split-and-restore edit can satisfy jointly.

confirmed.location: Both tabs — Endorser: "they see ... your endorsement strength"; Evaluator: "the endorsement strength they set, which is how strongly they backed that candidate"; implementation note: "real endorsement strengths mapped to the 10-90 display range"
confirmed.claim: Both tabs tell participants that evaluators see the strength the endorser set, but the implementation displays a 10-90 rescaling (displayConfidence of the raw value), so the number shown is literally not the number the endorser set. [sources: codex, mechanics]
confirmed.why: Breaches the literal-truthfulness constraint on both sides simultaneously — endorsers are promised their strength is shown, evaluators are told the displayed value is what the endorser set — and evaluators wager on a transformed signal whose compression can make very weak or very strong backing look less extreme.
confirmed.fix: Either display the raw 0-100 strength (the unipolar slider no longer needs the bipolar-era remap), or reword both sentences to avoid the identity claim (e.g., "a gauge of their endorsement strength") and describe the exact mapping; decide before fielding and amend suggestion 24 accordingly.
confirmed.verify_note: All three quotes are verbatim in the cited views, and the doc's own design notes (Endorser line 17, Evaluator line 118) commit to displaying displayConfidence(raw)=round(10+0.8*raw), so an endorser who sets 80 is shown as 74 (0 shows as 10, 100 as 90) — the displayed number is literally not "the endorsement strength they set," and suggestion 24 is what sharpened the evaluator-side wording into that identity claim (the endorser-side claim exists in the committed view too). No bracketed note resolves this for participants, the monotone-transform defense does not make the statement literally true, and the bipolar-era rationale for the 10-90 remap is indeed obsolete under the unipolar slider; given the stated hard literal-truthfulness constraint, fielding as written corrupts truthfulness for both N~100 endorsers and N~600 evaluators, so critical stands.

confirmed.location: Both tabs — Endorser: "Your candidate wins if they score higher ... and loses if they score lower"; Evaluator: "An endorsement is correct if the endorsed candidate scored higher ... in the same set"
confirmed.claim: Ties on the logical-reasoning test have no defined outcome or payment rule in any payoff — endorser component 1, evaluator wager settlement, and the evaluator-trust component are all silent on equal scores. [sources: codex, comprehension, mechanics]
confirmed.why: Unless ties are impossible by construction, the payment contract is incomplete; a backend rule that silently treats a tie as a loss, win, or excluded round would contradict or exceed the instructions, and on Prolific an undefined outcome in an incentive rule is a payment-dispute and truthfulness risk.
confirmed.fix: Either construct stimulus candidate sets only from pairs with strictly different logical-reasoning scores (and note this in the design notes), or state a single tie rule in both tabs and on outcome screens (e.g., "a tie counts as incorrect"); amend suggestions 7 and 31 at their respective definitions.
confirmed.verify_note: Confirmed: both quoted sentences appear verbatim in the accepted view (suggestions 7 and 31), and no participant-facing text or bracketed design note anywhere in either view defines or excludes ties on the 10-item logical-reasoning test, so the payment contract is genuinely incomplete across all three payoff components. Downgraded from critical to major because the Stage 3 note (outcome sequences pre-balanced, drawn from real win/loss outcomes) means fielded evaluator rounds cannot hit a tie, and candidate sets are researcher-constructed, so the only live exposure is a tied pair slipping into Stage 2 stimuli — a contingent edge case fixed by one documented line, not a systematic corruption of payments if fielded.

confirmed.location: Evaluator, allocation item 2: "endorsers at [ORGANIZATION 1: Atlas]" vs. Endorser tab where ORGANIZATION 1 is Vertex throughout
confirmed.claim: The organization placeholder is inconsistent: ORGANIZATION 1 is Vertex everywhere else in both tabs but Atlas in the org-level allocation item. [sources: codex, construct, comprehension, mechanics]
confirmed.why: If carried into the fielded survey, the evaluator would allocate organizational social capital to an organization they never saw, voiding the org-level DV and breaking the sponsorship link and the Stage 2/Stage 3 payment narrative; even as a placeholder slip it invites a piping error and confuses advisors reading the doc.
confirmed.fix: Use one dynamic organization token everywhere (change to [ORGANIZATION 1: Vertex] or a neutral [ENDORSER'S ORG]), and verify the fielded item pipes the yoked endorser's actual organization before displaying either allocation item.
confirmed.verify_note: Verified: allocation item 2 reads "[ORGANIZATION 1: Atlas]" in both accepted and committed views (line 173) while every other ORGANIZATION 1 instance is Vertex (7 uses in the Endorser tab), no suggestion touches it, and the line-174 design notes confirm the item is meant to name the endorser's own org, so the slip is real and not design intent. Downgraded from critical to major: the bracketed token's index (ORGANIZATION 1) still unambiguously specifies the correct pipe target and the payment claim stays literally true, so the doc invites a piping/mockup error and advisor confusion rather than guaranteeing corrupted data if fielded; fix by changing Atlas to Vertex and verifying the fielded item pipes the yoked endorser's actual org.

confirmed.location: Evaluator: "You have 10 future review slots ... how many would you allocate to seeing more endorsements from this endorser?"; Endorser: "they decide how much future review to allocate to you and to your organization"; design note: "no claim that this evaluator will see more candidate sets"
confirmed.claim: "Future review slots" and "seeing more endorsements" promise a review mechanism the design never implements: the only real consequence is a $0.05-per-slot cash transfer, no future review by anyone depends on the allocation, and the first-person stem invites the false belief that this evaluator will see more endorsements. [sources: codex, construct, comprehension, mechanics]
confirmed.why: Under the hard literal-truthfulness constraint, the same telegraph is made in both tabs (endorsers are told evaluators "decide how much future review to allocate to you"), so the DV's social-capital content — audience access — is asserted in wording but absent in mechanism, and participants may hold wrong beliefs about their own task.
confirmed.fix: Either commit in the protocol that allocation totals actually weight which endorsers are sampled for future evaluator sessions (one line of sampling code makes the wording literally true and makes the DV genuine audience access), or rename to something the payment alone makes true (e.g., "allocation slots") and reword both items to drop "future review" and "seeing more endorsements" in both tabs; amend suggestions 5, 9, 26, and 32.
confirmed.verify_note: All quotes verified verbatim in both views; no review/sampling mechanism exists anywhere in the doc — the sole implemented consequence is $0.05/slot (max $1.00 over 20 slots, arithmetic correct). The researcher-facing design note ("no claim that this evaluator will see more candidate sets") only defends the narrow first-person reading and is undercut by the actual item stem "allocate to seeing more endorsements from this endorser," which participants do see; endorsers are likewise told evaluators allocate "future review" with no mechanism behind it. Major, not critical: monetary incentive claims stay literally true, but the social-capital DV's audience-access content is wording-only, a real construct-validity and false-belief risk.

confirmed.location: Evaluator, allocation screens: "Each slot you allocate adds $0.05 to this endorser's bonus" (0-10 + 0-10 slots, no cost to the evaluator)
confirmed.claim: The allocation DV has zero opportunity cost: slots are free to give and unallocated slots have no stated use, so allocating everything is weakly dominant for any prosocial evaluator, collapsing the measure toward ceiling-prone costless generosity rather than scarce social-capital allocation. [sources: construct, mechanics]
confirmed.why: The focal comparison is by endorser gender, and dictator-game-style giving is reliably gender-differential, so a gender gap on allocations is confounded with altruism rather than accrued social capital; compressed variance at 10/10 also undercuts power, and "consequential by design" answers social desirability but not this rival explanation.
confirmed.fix: Create truthful scarcity — give withheld slots a real destination (e.g., "slots you do not allocate to this endorser go to other endorsers in the study") or let retained slots pay the evaluator $0.05; failing that, add a pre-registered warmth/likability covariate and pre-register ceiling handling (tobit/ordered or censoring-robustness models). Flag for the next design meeting rather than a silent wording edit; amend suggestion 32.
confirmed.verify_note: Verified against both views: the quoted allocation text appears verbatim, no cost to the evaluator or destination for withheld slots is ever stated, and the design note itself confirms slots are a pure transfer ("no claim that this evaluator will see more candidate sets") while addressing only social desirability, not opportunity cost. Arithmetic checks (20 x $0.05 = $1.00 cap, consistent across tabs), and the issue exists identically in the committed text, so suggestion 32 did not create it but a wording amendment alone cannot fix it. Major is correct: claims to participants stay literally true (not critical), but the costless-giving structure exposes a focal between-subjects DV to a recipient-gender generosity confound and ceiling compression.

confirmed.location: Evaluator, implementation note: "Endorser gender between-subjects, carried only by avatar color styling (Man blue #2563EB, Woman pink #EC4899)" plus final questions note "Manipulation check: analyze passers only."
confirmed.claim: Gender is carried solely by avatar hue, which confounds gender with color associations (blue carries trust/competence connotations, pink femininity but also lower status), may not be unambiguously perceived from the text alone, and will drive a low manipulation-check pass rate — so the mandated passers-only analysis conditions the sample on gender-attentiveness, a variable plausibly correlated with gender attitudes. [sources: codex, construct]
confirmed.why: Any evaluator-side treatment effect is attributable to pink-versus-blue styling, perceived gender, or stereotype salience rather than gender per se, and the passers-only subsample is selected on exactly the construct under study, threatening both internal validity and power (excluded non-passers are paid but unusable N).
confirmed.fix: Add an explicit gender cue while keeping the colors (a "Woman"/"Man" badge pill on the endorser card, or a gendered first name), or counterbalance color within gender; pretest that the avatar produces a unique, reliable gender interpretation, pilot the manipulation-check pass rate before committing the full N, and pre-register the expected exclusion rate.
confirmed.verify_note: Quotes are verbatim in both views, and the implementation confirms the badge pill reads "Endorser" with no gender word, so color styling is the sole cue. Pilot data (N=608, same manipulation) empirically confirms the risk: only 66.3% passed the gender manipulation check, and pass rates differed by arm (75.0% Woman vs 57.1% Man), so passers-only analysis conditions on a post-treatment variable that responds to treatment — a differential-selection threat the doc nowhere addresses. Major, not critical: it endangers validity and power but not payment truthfulness or data integrity.

confirmed.location: Evaluator, exit item 2: "...you had to endorse yourself to perform well on the logical reasoning test. How strongly would you endorse yourself?"
confirmed.claim: The self-endorsement exit item is ill-posed: "endorse yourself to perform well" reads as endorsing in order to perform, and no rival candidate, candidate set, or correctness criterion is defined, so the 0-100 response has no referent in a paradigm where strength means confidence of beating a specific rival. [sources: construct, comprehension]
confirmed.why: Responses will be uninterpretable noise, not comparable to endorser strengths, wasting the 4/16 exit-interview measure; participants who internalized the instructions (which the CQs enforce) are exactly the ones who will notice the missing win condition.
confirmed.fix: Reword to define the event, preserving the slider format: "Imagine you were a candidate in a future study like this one, and you set the endorsement strength for yourself: how strongly would you back yourself to score higher on the logical-reasoning test than the other organization's candidate?" Add "This question does not affect your pay."
confirmed.verify_note: The quote is verbatim in both views (identical, untouched by any suggestion), the "endorse yourself to perform well" clause is genuinely garbled, and the win condition (rival candidate in the same set) that the paradigm and CQ2 define as the slider's meaning is absent; the design note fixes only the slider format, which the participant never sees anyway. However, "no referent / uninterpretable noise" is overstated since "a future study like the one you just observed" imports much of the paradigm structure — the real damage is heterogeneous construal (absolute vs. relative performance) that degrades comparability to endorser strengths. Downgraded from major to minor: it is one hypothetical, unincentivized final exit item that cannot affect payments, truthfulness, or any focal DV; the fix is a one-sentence rewording like the one proposed.

confirmed.location: Endorser: "you always endorse the [ORGANIZATION 1: Vertex] candidate" / "Evaluators will see your endorsement as [Vertex] backing its own candidate"; Evaluator: "three decisions made by the same endorser, each with a new, independent set of candidates"
confirmed.claim: The design implements costly public organizational backing, not a canonical dyadic sponsor-protege relationship: the endorser cannot select a protege, the candidate rotates every round and gains nothing from being sponsored, and all consequential benefits flow to the endorser — so the tie the evaluator observes is endorser-to-organization, not sponsor-to-protege. [sources: codex, construct]
confirmed.why: Construct validity: reviewers will recognize this as organizational advocacy with skin in the game rather than sponsorship that advances a protege; the rotating-candidate feature is a defensible tradeoff (it isolates sponsor-level inference and avoids candidate-level confounds), but paper framing and the term "protege" must match what participants actually experienced.
confirmed.fix: In the write-up and pre-registration, frame the construct as organizationally mandated public sponsorship/advocacy and note rotating candidates as the mechanism isolating sponsor-level inference; restore the "assigned to represent" framing trimmed by suggestions 0, 3, and 19; if candidate advancement is essential to the construct, add a real candidate-facing consequence — wording alone cannot supply it.
confirmed.verify_note: All three quoted passages appear verbatim in the accepted view, and every payment clause in both tabs (including the [Payment mapping] and slot-telegraph design notes) confirms all endorsement-contingent money flows to the endorser while the candidate rotates each round and receives nothing — so the observed tie is endorser-to-organization, exactly as claimed, and no design note resolves it. Suggestions 0, 3, and 19 do trim the "assigned to represent"/"you represent" framing (suggestion 3's replacement even makes the org the actor: "Vertex backing its own candidate"). Major is right: it directly answers Jose's construct-validity question 1 and threatens paper framing, but would not corrupt data, payments, or truthfulness if fielded.

confirmed.location: Endorser tab, opening: "You are an endorser for [ORGANIZATION 1: Vertex]."
confirmed.claim: The accepted opening drops "assigned to represent": endorsers are never told the affiliation is assigned rather than chosen, the word "represent" (used in endorser CQ2's keyed answer) is never taught before that check, and the Evaluator tab still says endorsers were "each assigned to represent an organization," leaving the tabs asymmetric. [sources: comprehension, fidelity]
confirmed.why: A naive reader stalls on the cold open (What is Vertex? Why am I its endorser?) and may infer the pairing is merit-based; the CQ2 keyed answer uses vocabulary the accepted text never introduces; exogenous assignment is load-bearing for how endorsers construe the must-endorse obligation.
confirmed.fix: Amend suggestion 0's insert to "You are an endorser for [ORGANIZATION 1: Vertex], an organization you have been assigned to represent in this study." One clause restores assignment, teaches "represent," and keeps the shorter opening.
confirmed.verify_note: All three sub-claims verify against the text: the accepted endorser tab contains "assigned" nowhere and "represent" only inside CQ2's keyed answer (suggestions 0, 3, 5, 19 stripped it), while the evaluator tab still says "each assigned to represent an organization." But the severity is overstated: CQ2 remains uniquely answerable from "The candidate from [Vertex]" alone, the accepted text still frames Vertex as "your organization" in six places so the sponsorship role is not lost, assignment is the only plausible construal for a participant handed the role at survey start, and no participant-facing claim becomes untrue — leaving a real fidelity drop with a cheap one-clause fix, which is friction, not a comprehension or validity risk.

confirmed.location: Endorser: "Use the slider to set your endorsement strength: how confident you are that your organization's candidate will score higher ... and how much you are willing to put behind them" plus the linear win/lose payment rule
confirmed.claim: Endorsement strength is not an incentive-compatible confidence report: the linear payoff makes corner strengths optimal for a risk-neutral endorser, and the evaluator-trust component rewards inflating displayed strength, so the variable conflates belief, advocacy, risk preference, and signaling; suggestion 25's removal of "well-calibrated" is correct and should stand. [sources: codex, fidelity]
confirmed.why: Variation in strength cannot be cleanly interpreted as calibrated probability or sponsorship intensity, which matters because evaluator trust is conditioned on the displayed strength; restoring calibration language would breach literal truthfulness given the payout rule.
confirmed.fix: Interpret the variable narrowly as "wagered backing" in analysis and framing, never a calibrated probability; if calibrated belief is required, add a separate probability estimate under a proper scoring rule; accept suggestion 25 as the truthful ceiling and do not restore "well-calibrated."
confirmed.verify_note: Verified: the quoted slider instruction and linear win/lose rule appear verbatim in the accepted Endorser view (lines 22, 48); EV = 0.50 + 0.50s(2p−1) is linear in s, so corner strengths are optimal for a risk-neutral endorser, and component 2 ($1 × evaluator wager on a win) adds a genuine strength-inflation incentive since the design itself presumes wagers respond to displayed strength. The committed text's "well-calibrated" (pending suggestion 25 deletes it) is not literally true under this payoff, so the finding correctly identifies 25 as load-bearing for the truthfulness constraint; no design note resolves the incentive-compatibility gap, and major is right because the risk lands on suggestion-25 rejection and on analysis/framing that reads strength as calibrated belief, not on the accepted view as written.

confirmed.location: Evaluator: "Your task is to judge how much you trust one endorser" / "If their candidate wins, the more you wager, the larger their bonus" plus fielded opening "can affect that participant's pay" and CQ7
confirmed.claim: The wager is not a pure trust measure: it moves both the evaluator's own risky payoff and, on a win, the endorser's payoff, and the other-regarding channel is made maximally salient (opening line plus a must-pass CQ), so gender differences in wagers could reflect social preferences, risk attitudes, altruism, or impression management rather than trust updating. [sources: codex, construct]
confirmed.why: Calling the measure "trust" overstates identification, and prosociality is a rival account for level differences by gender — though notably not for the focal prediction: chivalrous prosociality implies amplified upward updating for women, not symmetric slope muting, so the design can discriminate if that is made explicit.
confirmed.fix: Label the primary construct "wager" or "costly reliance" (or add a separate non-payment-bearing trust rating, or decouple endorser pay from the focal wager); pre-register the discriminating prediction (prosociality implies level and upward-slope asymmetries; the hypothesis implies symmetric slope muting) and add a funneled suspicion probe after the gender manipulation check.
confirmed.verify_note: All four quoted locations verified verbatim in the accepted view (lines 96, 104, 107, 146-148) and the mechanics check out: the wager both sets the evaluator's own risky payoff and transfers $1.00 x wager% to the endorser on a win, with that channel made salient by the opening line, a dedicated paragraph, and must-pass CQ7, and no design note adds a non-incentivized trust rating, suspicion probe, or discriminating prediction. The finding actually understates the risk: a constant chivalry/gift component in wagers toward women would mechanically attenuate delta_wager, so prosociality is a rival account for the focal symmetric slope-muting prediction too, not just for levels. Major (not critical) because nothing corrupts data or payments; it is an interpretation/construct-validity risk with cheap, truthfulness-compatible fixes.

confirmed.location: Evaluator header note: "target N depends on the outcome-sequence cell structure (to be fixed at the next meeting)"; Endorser design note: "verify Stage 3 cell supply in pilot data"
confirmed.claim: The focal outcome-sequence design is not yet field-ready: sequence cells, power for the once-per-person allocations, and supply of real endorser decisions are all unresolved. [sources: codex]
confirmed.why: The focal bidirectionally-muted-updating hypothesis requires adequate support for positive and negative updating balanced across gender; "at least one hit and at least one miss" does not guarantee balanced win-to-loss and loss-to-win transitions or adequate cells.
confirmed.fix: Lock and power the outcome sequences, verify real-stream supply in every gender x strength x sequence cell, and define a no-supply fallback before fielding.
confirmed.verify_note: Both quoted notes appear verbatim in both views (accepted/committed lines 17, 85), and line 118 independently confirms the sequence set/cell structure is deferred and stream supply is only "where supply allows." The doc acknowledges but does not resolve any of the three gaps, so this is not "already handled"; the hit-and-miss constraint indeed leaves 6 of 8 three-round sequences unspecified, so transition balance per cell is genuinely open. Major (not critical) is correct: real validity risk to the focal muted-updating hypothesis if fielded as written, but no payment/truthfulness corruption.

confirmed.location: Evaluator: "You will evaluate three decisions made by the same endorser, each with a new, independent set of candidates."; implementation note: "Outcome sequences pre-balanced (every participant sees at least one hit and at least one miss)."
confirmed.claim: "Independent" conflicts with deliberately constrained sequence sampling: "new" can be true, but the displayed outcome sequence is deliberately constrained across rounds, so the rounds are not independently sampled. [sources: codex]
confirmed.why: An avoidable literal-truthfulness problem that may lead participants to infer natural random sampling.
confirmed.fix: Delete "independent" and retain "each with a new set of candidates." Amend suggestion 28.
confirmed.verify_note: Quotes are accurate and the sampling constraint is real (pre-balanced sequences exclude HHH/MMM, so displayed outcomes are conditionally dependent), but the literal-truthfulness charge fails: "independent" modifies the candidate sets, which genuinely are new, non-overlapping pairs with causally independent performances, and the accepted text deliberately dropped the OLD baseline's "randomly selected" subset claim, so no false sampling statement exists. What survives is an avoidable i.i.d. implicature fixable by deleting one word from suggestion 28 (note "independent" also appears in the committed text, so the fix must amend, not reject) — friction, not a validity or comprehension risk, and arm-symmetric for the focal contrast.

confirmed.location: Evaluator: "decide how much of your own compensation to wager", later clarified by "For each decision, you start with a $0.50 bank."
confirmed.claim: "Your own compensation" can imply guaranteed participation pay is at risk, since the sentence does not distinguish the three $0.50 bonus banks from base compensation. [sources: codex, comprehension]
confirmed.why: A naive, payment-anxious Prolific participant may believe unsuccessful wagers can reduce their guaranteed study payment.
confirmed.fix: Change "your own compensation" to "a $0.50 study-bonus bank for each decision" (or "your own bonus money"). Amend suggestion 20.
confirmed.verify_note: The quoted phrase does appear (accepted view lines 100 and 104, via suggestions 20 AND 24 — the fix cites only 20), and in isolation "your own compensation" is indeed broader than the OLD baseline's more precise "your own bonus" (OLD line 209), so the momentary misreading is possible. But it cannot be major: before any wager the participant-facing text fully bounds the stakes ("you start with a $0.50 bank... Wagering 0% means you keep your $0.50 no matter what"; opening line 96 says decisions "determine your own bonus"), and mandatory CQs 4-6 enforce the bank mechanics — so no belief that base pay is at risk survives to a decision; also note the phrase comes from the committed redesign text, not the simplification pass, making this transient reading friction (minor), fixable cheaply in both suggestions 20 and 24.

confirmed.location: Evaluator design note: "Also collect evaluator gender in-survey (participant_female is a mandated covariate...)" vs. listed final questions (endorser-gender manipulation check and self-endorsement item only)
confirmed.claim: The mandated evaluator-gender covariate is only a design note, not an implemented item: no evaluator-gender question appears in the documented fielded flow. [sources: codex]
confirmed.why: The stated mandated control (participant_female) cannot be constructed from the documented fielded flow.
confirmed.fix: Add the actual evaluator-gender item and response options to the final-question flow.
confirmed.verify_note: Verified in both views: the Final-questions flow lists only the endorser-gender manipulation check and the self-endorsement item, and evaluator gender exists only in the bracketed note at line 181 — the quote and factual claim are accurate. But the note is an explicit, imperative spec instruction ("collect evaluator gender in-survey... do not rely on Prolific demographics alone"), so the covariate is already mandated in the doc itself and this is not a participant-facing gap; only the verbatim item wording/options are missing. That is doc-completeness friction (fix: write out the item), not a real validity risk — downgrade from major to minor.

confirmed.location: Evaluator design note: "Org and sponsor allocations are collinear by design ... analyze separately, never as competing predictors"; both allocation stems: "Each slot you allocate adds $0.05 to this endorser's bonus."
confirmed.claim: The two allocation outcomes are not behaviorally or economically independent — both reward the same person, appear consecutively, and the org allocation creates no distinct organizational consequence — and it is counterintuitive that slots given to the ORGANIZATION pay THIS endorser, which makes item 2 read like a misprint of item 1. [sources: codex, comprehension]
confirmed.why: The organization item can reflect anchoring, consistency, or extra generosity toward the individual rather than clean reputational spillover, and confused participants may second-guess item 1 or treat item 2 as a duplicate.
confirmed.fix: Randomize item order, analyze the outcomes separately as already noted, avoid claiming the org allocation uniquely identifies organizational reputation (a distinct organizational recipient would be needed for stronger separation), and append an explanation such as "(This endorser is the only [Vertex] endorser in your session, so these slots also add to their bonus.)" — true given one sponsor per participant.
confirmed.verify_note: Verified both quotes verbatim (design note at line 174; identical "$0.05 to this endorser's bonus" sentence on both allocation stems at lines 171/173 in both views). The economic claim holds: both DVs pay the same endorser at the same rate with no organizational recipient, and no participant-facing text explains why org slots pay this individual — the resolution lives only in the researcher-facing bracket, and the note's "read the org item as reputational spillover" overclaims what an economically identical, consecutively placed item can identify. "Reads like a misprint" is slightly overstated (the fact is disclosed three times), but the validity risk to a focal DV plus the unexplained payee justify major, not critical.

confirmed.location: Endorser: "Use the links below to familiarize yourself..." (export shows only "[WORD TASKS] [KNOWLEDGE TASKS][LOGIC TASKS]"); both tabs: repeated "Proposed:" labels with no screen text
confirmed.claim: Core screens and links cannot be verified from the supplied source: the text files do not preserve link targets or the proposed slider/outcome/avatar screens (possibly an export limitation rather than a doc defect). [sources: codex]
confirmed.why: Slider labels, transformed-strength display, outcome feedback, candidate IDs, organization identity, and gender cues are central to comprehension and truthfulness.
confirmed.fix: Perform a rendered Google Doc/Qualtrics QA pass and verify every visible label, link, organization token, and numeric value against these instructions.
confirmed.verify_note: Verified in both views: line 43's "Use the links below..." is followed only by bare tokens [WORD TASKS][KNOWLEDGE TASKS][LOGIC TASKS] with no targets, and the "Proposed:" screen slots (Endorser lines 52-77, Evaluator lines 155-165, including the Woman-arm avatar screen) are empty in the text export, so the slider/outcome/avatar screens and links genuinely cannot be QA'd from the supplied source. Design notes give intended colors and display mapping but not rendered screen content, so the participant-facing gap is unresolved; since those screens carry the entire gender manipulation and the wager UI, major (not minor) is warranted, though it is a verification gap rather than a confirmed defect, so not critical.

confirmed.location: Both tabs vs. OLD — OLD: "used a slider to predict which candidate would score higher"; Accepted: "you always endorse the [ORGANIZATION 1: Vertex] candidate" and "the sum of all three (up to $3.00)"
confirmed.claim: The accepted view is faithful to the committed redesign, but both depart substantially from OLD: free A/B prediction became must-endorse own-organization backing, bipolar choice became unipolar strength, one-or-two endorsers became one, random-decision payment became the sum of three $0.50 banks, and allocation outcomes were added. [sources: codex]
confirmed.why: The suggestion pass itself is mostly wording simplification, but the resulting experiment is not a close procedural replication of OLD, so comparability with the original paradigm is limited relative to the "minimal deviation" objective.
confirmed.fix: Treat these as intentional redesign decisions in the protocol and change log; do not describe the full accepted design as merely a simplified version of OLD.
confirmed.verify_note: All quoted text and all five enumerated departures from OLD check out verbatim (free choice→must-endorse, bipolar→unipolar, 1-2 endorsers→1, random-decision $2 payment→sum of three $0.50 banks max $3.00, allocation DVs added), and the accepted view is indeed faithful to the committed text. But every departure is an intentional, already-documented redesign decision (design notes: "must-endorse resolution of the May 30 fork," "unipolar replaces the bipolar A/B slider," allocations as "continuous version of the 4/16 items"), so the finding identifies no defect, risks nothing if fielded, and rejects no suggestion — it is a correct but purely documentation/framing caution answering the deviation-from-OLD question, warranting minor, not major.

confirmed.location: Endorser tab: "One of your endorsements is picked at random, along with one evaluator who reviewed it." and "Evaluators (participants in a separate study) review your endorsements."
confirmed.claim: The payment mapping is undefined when the randomly selected endorsement has no reviewer, and the categorical claim that evaluators review the endorser's endorsements is not guaranteed true: each evaluator sees only 3 of 10 decisions and streams are sampled by cell, so some endorsements — possibly some endorsers — may never be reviewed. [sources: mechanics]
confirmed.why: If an unreviewed endorsement is drawn, components 2 and 3 have no evaluator to compute from, so either the mechanic silently zeroes out (making the promised three-part structure false) or the stated selection rule is not followed — either way the hard truthful-yoking constraint is violated. Suggestions 4 and 5 made this worse by dropping the committed view's hedges.
confirmed.fix: Add one design-note sentence: selection is uniform over the endorser's endorsements that received at least one evaluator, and Stage 3 assignment must guarantee every endorser has at least one reviewed endorsement. Amend the participant sentence minimally to "For each endorsement they review, they see your organization, the candidate you endorsed, and your endorsement strength."
confirmed.verify_note: Both quotes verified in the accepted view. The bracketed payment-mapping note supports joint pair-selection (defined whenever the endorser has >=1 reviewed endorsement) but nothing in either view guarantees every endorser is reviewed, and the {strong, weak}-tercile cell sampling structurally guarantees some endorsements (all mid-tercile ones) are never reviewed, so the categorical claim and the selection rule are not guaranteed literally true under the hard truthful-yoking constraint. Suggestions 4+5 did drop the committed hedge "For each endorsement that is shown"; severity stays major (not critical) because the design note admits a truthful implementation and the zero-reviewer failure is preventable at assignment time with the proposed one-sentence fix.

confirmed.location: Endorser tab: "2. Evaluator trust. If your candidate wins, you also earn $1.00 times the evaluator's wager percentage, up to $1.00."
confirmed.claim: Suggestion 8 drops the sentence "The more they trust your endorsement, the more you earn." [sources: fidelity]
confirmed.why: That sentence is the only place the sponsor's incentive text makes the audience-trust channel psychologically salient; the formula alone reads as a payout rule, not a reason to court evaluator trust — losing it can mute the impression-management motive and shift the strength distributions that become Stage 3 stimuli, weakening the sponsorship construct on the sponsor side.
confirmed.fix: Accept the compression but append the sentence back: "...up to $1.00. The more the evaluator trusts your endorsement, the more you earn."
confirmed.verify_note: Suggestion 8 does drop "The more they trust your endorsement, the more you earn" (confirmed in committed line 23 vs accepted line 23), but the harm claim fails: the accepted heading is literally "2. Evaluator trust.", the retained formula ($1.00 x wager%) states the same monotonic relationship, and endorser CQ1 forces computation of the evaluator-wager component, so no trust salience or incentive content is actually lost. The impression-management (strength-signals-confidence) gloss the reviewer worries about belongs to suggestion 18's deletion, not 8 — keeping the sentence is a prose-emphasis preference, a nit.

confirmed.location: Endorser tab: "High strength is strong public backing: it earns you more if your candidate wins, and costs you more if your candidate loses. Low strength is safer..."
confirmed.claim: Suggestion 18 drops both audience-signaling clauses ("shows the evaluator you are putting your money where your mouth is"; "signals weaker backing") and replaces the calibration cue "protects you when you are unsure" with the bare "is safer." [sources: fidelity]
confirmed.why: The objective screen now describes a pure financial-risk choice with no audience; the signaling clauses are what frame strength as PUBLIC backing observed by an evaluator (the core sponsorship construct), and "when you are unsure" is the only cue tying low strength to genuine uncertainty rather than timidity. Both claims are literally true under the design, so nothing forced their removal.
confirmed.fix: Amend: "High strength is strong public backing: it earns you more if your candidate wins, costs you more if your candidate loses, and shows the evaluator you are putting your money where your mouth is. Low strength is safer when you are unsure: it earns less if your candidate wins, but risks less if your candidate loses."
confirmed.verify_note: Suggestion 18 verifiably drops both clauses and softens "protects you when you are unsure" to "is safer," so the fidelity deviation is real and flaggable under Jose's minimal-deviation mandate. But the finding's severity rationale is overstated: the accepted screen still says "strong public backing," strength is still defined as confidence in the same sentence (and at line 16, "less confident, less at risk"), and the evaluator audience plus the signaling incentive survive explicitly at lines 16, 18, and 23 (evaluator sees strength; evaluator wager pays the endorser). The drop removes redundant emphasis, not substance, so it is minor, not major.

confirmed.location: Evaluator tab, task paragraph: "...and the endorsement strength they set, which is how strongly they backed that candidate."
confirmed.claim: The evaluator is never told the scale of endorsement strength — no range or anchors are given, so a displayed value like "strength 72" is uninterpretable from the text alone. [sources: comprehension]
confirmed.why: The wager DV is a direct function of how the evaluator reads the strength number; the OLD baseline explicitly explained the slider, and both the committed and accepted redesign texts dropped any scale description, so early-round wagers add noise exactly where the design needs signal.
confirmed.fix: In the id-24 insert, add a parenthetical: "...and the endorsement strength they set (on a scale where 0 is the weakest endorsement and 100 the strongest), which is how strongly they backed that candidate" — coordinating with the display-mapping fix so the stated scale matches what is shown.
confirmed.verify_note: Confirmed: the evaluator tab in both accepted and committed views never states the endorsement-strength scale (no range, no anchors; accepted even drops the committed view's lone "slider" mention), while the OLD baseline explicitly explained "slider position (0-100)... distance from 50 reflects confidence." The [design note] mapping display to 10-90 is researcher-facing only and worsens rather than resolves the gap, and no comprehension check covers the scale. Since the wager DV and the strong/weak tercile manipulation both hinge on evaluators interpreting the displayed number, this is a real comprehension/validity risk — major is the right severity.

confirmed.location: Evaluator, accepted text (suggestion 23): "Their endorsement strength showed how confident they were that their candidate would score higher..."
confirmed.claim: Suggestion 23 tells evaluators that strength equals sincere confidence, but the disclosed incentives (endorsers earn more when evaluators wager more) give endorsers an inflation motive, making the sentence potentially false for some endorsers and internally inconsistent with the "how strongly they backed" framing one paragraph later. [sources: construct, mechanics]
confirmed.why: Telling evaluators strength IS confidence pre-resolves the exact belief-versus-advocacy inference that makes this sponsorship rather than forecasting, and risks a literal-truth problem if endorsers strategically overclaim.
confirmed.fix: Amend suggestion 23's final clause to the advocacy framing suggestion 24 already uses: "Their endorsement strength showed how strongly they backed their candidate to score higher on the logical-reasoning test than the other organization's candidate in the same set."
confirmed.verify_note: Quote verified at accepted line 103, and the mechanics check out: the linear performance stake plus the disclosed evaluator-wager coupling (line 107) make strength inflation rational even at p=0.5, so "showed how confident they were" is not incentive-guaranteed, and the confidence-vs-"how strongly they backed" mismatch with line 104 arises specifically from accepting suggestions 23+24 together. Attenuating context the reviewer missed: the confidence framing is inherited verbatim from the committed text and the OLD baseline (not introduced by suggestion 23), and the Stage 2 tab elicits strength as confidence-plus-backing, so the proposed advocacy-only rewording would deviate further from the committed/OLD text than suggestion 23 does. Real but low-stakes framing friction with a one-clause fix; minor is correct.

confirmed.location: Endorser tab: "Evaluators will see your endorsement as [ORGANIZATION 1: Vertex] backing its own candidate."
confirmed.claim: Suggestion 3 shifts the perceived agent from person to organization (replacing "a [Vertex] endorser backing their own organization's candidate"), depersonalizing the sponsor at exactly the point where the endorser should understand that they, personally, are doing public backing and will personally accrue the evaluator's wagers and allocations; the Evaluator tab keeps person-level framing, so the tabs now frame it differently. [sources: construct, fidelity]
confirmed.why: The social-capital DVs are person-level (slots pay the endorser); the endorser's sense of personal advocacy is part of the sponsorship construct on the Stage 2 side, and the committed wording carried it.
confirmed.fix: Amend suggestion 3's last sentence to keep brevity but restore the personal agent: "Evaluators will see you, a [ORGANIZATION 1: Vertex] endorser, backing your organization's candidate."
confirmed.verify_note: Verified: suggestion 3 does replace "a [Vertex] endorser backing their own organization's candidate" (committed line 16) with "[Vertex] backing its own candidate" (accepted line 16), shifting the perceived agent from person to organization, while the Evaluator tab keeps person-level framing ("trust one endorser") — so the deviation and cross-tab mismatch are real. The "exactly the point" rhetoric is overstated (the immediately following sentence and the whole earnings section remain fully person-level: "your endorsements," "allocate to you"), so impact is buffered; minor is the correct severity — a genuine meaning shift relevant to the sponsorship construct, not mere style, but no real validity risk.

confirmed.location: Evaluator, accepted text (suggestion 24): "the endorsement strength they set..." vs. the current decision-screen label (mockups and live survey still read "Endorser's confidence")
confirmed.claim: The instructions define the displayed number as "endorsement strength" but the screens participants actually see label it "Endorser's confidence" — a terminology mismatch between instructions and stimuli that comprehension checks cannot catch. [sources: construct, fidelity]
confirmed.why: Participants meet an on-screen term the instructions never defined, and "confidence" undercuts the advocacy construct the redesign is built around; CQ-trained participants are exactly the ones who will notice.
confirmed.fix: Accept suggestion 24, then relabel the decision-screen field to "Endorsement strength" in the mockups and the live survey before fielding (already flagged as pending in the project's own notes); no doc text change needed.
confirmed.verify_note: Confirmed: suggestion 24 removes the only instruction-text instance of "endorser's confidence" and replaces it with "the endorsement strength they set," while the mockup PNGs (4 instances per HANDOFF.md), the doc-embedded mockups, and the live Qualtrics decision screens all still label the field "Endorser's confidence" — a mismatch the project's own notes flag as pending. Mildly overstated in one respect (accepted line 103 says strength "showed how confident they were," so the confidence concept is defined and participants can bridge), which is why this is friction, not a comprehension risk: minor stands. The fix (accept 24, relabel screens before fielding) is correct; rejecting 24 instead would restore screen consistency but break the doc's otherwise-uniform "endorsement strength" terminology.

confirmed.location: Evaluator, implementation note: "Streams are real endorsers sampled by cell (gender x tercile x outcome sequence), matched across gender arms on candidate sets where supply allows."
confirmed.claim: Organization identity is absent from the sampling-cell definition: the displayed org name (and any org badge styling) can correlate with gender arm, and nothing specifies that org badge colors must avoid the blue/pink hues reserved for the gender cue. [sources: construct]
confirmed.why: An org-name/gender imbalance would confound the gender manipulation with org identity, and org badges rendered in blue or pink would contaminate the only carrier of the gender manipulation.
confirmed.fix: Add to the note: "displayed org held constant (or balanced) across gender arms; org badge styling uses gender-neutral hues (no blue/pink family)."
confirmed.verify_note: Quote is verbatim from the implementation note (line 118, both views), and the gap is real: the sampling cell is only gender x tercile x outcome sequence, org identity is shown to evaluators (lines 104, 173) but never required to be constant/balanced across gender arms, and no org styling constraint exists anywhere. However, the existing "matched across gender arms on candidate sets where supply allows" clause implicitly matches orgs wherever it succeeds, and the badge-hue concern is about unspecified styling, so this is a one-line hardening of a researcher-facing note — minor, not major.

confirmed.location: Endorser tab, screens 1-2: "Each candidate set has two candidates..." / "You will see the available quiz and word search performance information..."
confirmed.claim: The concepts candidate, candidate set, quiz, word search, and logical reasoning test are all used on the first two screens but not defined until the "Who are the candidates?" section, which comes after the earnings rules and after CQ1-CQ2; the id-1 insert sharpened this pre-existing order problem by naming the specific tasks. [sources: comprehension]
confirmed.why: A first-time reader hits "quiz and word search performance information" with no idea what the tasks are or who candidates are.
confirmed.fix: Add one forward-reference sentence to screen 1: "Candidates are earlier participants who completed several paid tasks; you will learn more about them and the tasks shortly." (Or move the "Who are the candidates?" section before the earnings section.)
confirmed.verify_note: Verified in the accepted view: screen 1 uses "candidate set," "quiz," "word search," and "logical reasoning test" undefined (line 14-15), and the defining "Who are the candidates?" section (line 38) comes after earnings (21-25) and CQ1-CQ2 (27-36); the id-1 insert did replace committed "professional ability tests" with the specific undefined task names, sharpening a pre-existing ordering issue. Minor is right: CQ1-CQ2 are still answerable from prior text and definitions arrive before any decision screen, so it is first-read friction, not a validity or payment risk.

confirmed.location: Endorser tab: "Evaluators will see your endorsement as [ORGANIZATION 1: Vertex] backing its own candidate."
confirmed.claim: "Evaluators" is used on the slider screen before it is defined two paragraphs later ("Evaluators (participants in a separate study) review your endorsements"). [sources: comprehension]
confirmed.why: First-mention stall: the naive reader does not yet know evaluators exist or that they are people in another study.
confirmed.fix: Move the parenthetical to first mention: "Evaluators (participants in a separate study) will see your endorsement as [Vertex] backing its own candidate," and drop it from the later paragraph.
confirmed.verify_note: Quote is verbatim in the accepted view and "Evaluators" is genuinely used before its "(participants in a separate study)" definition, so the finding survives; but the intervening paragraph is a researcher-facing design note, so the participant-facing definition arrives in the immediately next paragraph, and the same ordering pre-exists in the committed view (not introduced by suggestions 3/4). A one-sentence, self-resolving stall with no decision, CQ, or incentive claim in between is style-level ordering, not real friction: downgrade minor to nit.

confirmed.location: Evaluator tab: "For this endorser's payment, one endorsement and one evaluator who reviewed it are selected at random." vs. "Your bonus from these three decisions is the sum of all three (up to $3.00)."
confirmed.claim: Two different payment rules (random selection for the ENDORSER's pay; sum-of-three for the evaluator's OWN bonus) are taught nine lines apart with no explicit contrast, and CQ6's distractor "One randomly selected decision" is exactly this conflation; the text never states that the evaluator's own bonus does not depend on the selection. [sources: comprehension]
confirmed.why: CQ6/CQ7 remain uniquely answerable on careful reading, but this is the most likely screen-out trap in the set, and payment-anxious Prolific workers may believe their own bonus is lottery-contingent.
confirmed.fix: After the sum-of-three sentence (id-31 insert), add: "(The random selection described earlier affects only the endorser's pay. Your own bonus is always the sum of your three decisions.)"
confirmed.verify_note: Both quotes appear verbatim in the accepted view (lines 108 and 117, exactly nine lines apart), and the text indeed never states the evaluator's own sum-of-three bonus is independent of the random selection — the accepted view's "For this endorser's payment" scoping is only an implicit mitigation. CQ6's distractor "One randomly selected decision" is precisely this conflation and was the true rule in the OLD baseline paradigm, making it a plausible trap for experienced workers under a must-pass-all screen-out; but since both CQs stay uniquely answerable from the text and all payment claims are truthful, this is friction, so minor stands.

confirmed.location: Evaluator tab, Endorsers paragraph: "...than the other organization's candidate in the same set."
confirmed.claim: "Set" is never defined in the evaluator tab before use, yet CQ2's keyed answer hinges on the phrase "in the same candidate set." [sources: comprehension]
confirmed.why: Inferable but a stall; the keyed answer should not use a term the instructions never introduced.
confirmed.fix: In the id-23 insert: "Each decision showed an endorser two candidates (one 'candidate set'): one from their own organization and one from another organization..."
confirmed.verify_note: Confirmed: in the accepted evaluator tab, "set" first appears bare in the id-23 Endorsers paragraph and the compound "candidate set" occurs only inside CQ2's keyed answer; the term is defined only in the Endorser tab, which evaluators never see, and the design notes don't resolve it for participants. The gap exists in the committed view too (pre-existing, not suggestion-introduced), and the meaning is inferable from "two candidates" plus the near-verbatim correctness sentence, so the keyed answer stays uniquely defensible — friction at a must-pass CQ, hence minor, not major.

confirmed.location: Endorser tab, candidates section: "[ORGANIZATION 1: Vertex] is your organization's candidate, [ORGANIZATION 2: Beacon] is the other candidate."
confirmed.claim: The id-17 compression created a category error — it literally equates the organization with the candidate. [sources: comprehension]
confirmed.why: Readers will mostly recover, but it reads as a mistake and slows exactly the reader the simplification pass is for.
confirmed.fix: "...the candidate from [Vertex] is your organization's candidate; the candidate from [Beacon] is the other organization's."
confirmed.verify_note: The quoted sentence appears verbatim in the accepted view (line 41), and the id-17 suggestion pair confirms the compression dropped "the candidate affiliated with" from the committed text ("the candidate affiliated with [Vertex] is your organization's candidate"), leaving a sentence that literally equates the organization with the candidate. No bracketed design note resolves it — participants would see the malformed sentence as-is; the intended elliptical reading is recoverable and the must-endorse mapping is restated correctly elsewhere (e.g. "one from [Vertex] (your organization's candidate)"), so it is a parse stumble, not a comprehension or validity risk. Minor (friction, not mere style, since the sentence is literally false as written in participant-facing text) is the correct severity.

confirmed.location: Endorser objective sentence (id 18), endorser-incentive sentence (id 25), allocation intro sentence (id 32)
confirmed.claim: Three sentences exceed the ~30-word ceiling: the endorser objective sentence (39 words), the endorser-incentive sentence (36 words), and the allocation intro sentence (32 words). [sources: comprehension]
confirmed.why: These are the densest payoff-logic sentences in the doc; length is where average-reading-level participants drop the conditional structure.
confirmed.fix: Split each at the colon/comma, e.g. id 25 → "Their pay works like a wager. A stronger endorsement earned more if their candidate scored higher on the logical-reasoning test than the other organization's candidate in that set. It earned less if their candidate scored lower." (Note past tense: the endorsements already happened.)
confirmed.verify_note: Recounted all three sentences in the accepted view: id 18 first sentence = exactly 39 words, id 25 wager sentence = 36, id 32 allocation sentence = 32, so the counts and locations are accurate, and the committed versions are even longer so the suggestions did not already fix this. The ~30-word ceiling is a readability heuristic rather than a doc requirement and the sentences are colon-chunked, but these are the load-bearing payoff sentences behind must-pass comprehension checks, so minor (friction) is the right severity — not nit, not major.

confirmed.location: Endorser tab, "Who are the candidates?" section and the following profile paragraph (suggestions 15 and 17)
confirmed.claim: Suggestions 15 and 17 are an accept-together pair: the "base your endorsement strength on the quiz and word-search scores" instruction is deleted by 15 and re-inserted (compressed) by 17. [sources: fidelity]
confirmed.why: If 15 is accepted and 17 rejected, the instruction telling endorsers what to base their decision on vanishes entirely; if 17 is accepted and 15 rejected, it appears twice. Meaning is preserved only under joint acceptance.
confirmed.fix: Accept both together (both are fine as written); do not split the pair.
confirmed.verify_note: Verified against both views and the suggestion JSON: suggestion 15's delete removes the "base your endorsement strength on the quiz and word search scores" sentences (committed line 39) and its insert drops them; suggestion 17's insert re-adds a compressed version (accepted line 41) that its own deleted text never contained — so the pair is genuinely accept-together (15-only loses the explicit evidence-basis instruction from the whole endorser tab; 17-only duplicates it within one section). Slight overstatement only in "vanishes entirely," since suggestion 2's insert still gives the criterion ("base your strength on how likely your candidate is to score higher... on the logical reasoning test") though not the quiz/word-search evidence basis; that residual coverage is exactly why minor, not major, is the right severity.

confirmed.location: Evaluator tab: "If your session is selected, your wager on that endorsement and your allocations directly determine part of this endorser's pay."
confirmed.claim: Suggestion 27 changes plural "your wagers" to singular "your wager on that endorsement" — a substantive change, but a truthfulness fix, not drift. [sources: fidelity]
confirmed.why: Only the wager placed on the randomly selected endorsement feeds the endorser's pay; the committed plural overstated the consequence of all three wagers.
confirmed.fix: Accept as-is (an improvement; flagged so it is not mistaken for meaning loss).
confirmed.verify_note: Verified against suggestion 27's insert/delete pair and both doc views: the committed text says plural "your wagers ... directly determine part of this endorser's pay" while the accepted text narrows to "your wager on that endorsement," matching the payment mapping (only the wager on the randomly selected endorsement feeds component 2; both allocations always count). The claim is accurate — a substantive but truth-tightening change, correctly flagged as accept-as-is under the brief's mandate to flag all substantive alterations; minor is the right calibration since no fix is needed.

confirmed.location: Endorser tab, earnings intro: "One of your endorsements is picked at random..."
confirmed.claim: The endorser is never told how many candidate sets they will judge (k=10 lives only in the design notes), so "one of your endorsements" is the first hint there are several. [sources: comprehension]
confirmed.why: Minor stall and expectation-setting gap; stating the count also makes the random-selection rule concrete.
confirmed.fix: Screen 1 or the earnings intro: "You will review 10 candidate sets. One of your 10 endorsements is picked at random..."
confirmed.verify_note: Confirmed: k=10 appears only in the bracketed design note (accepted view line 17) and no participant-facing Endorser-tab sentence in either view states the number of candidate sets, so the gap is real and uncured. The finding's "first hint there are several" phrasing is slightly off (lines 14 and 18 already imply plurality via "Each candidate set" and "your endorsements... For each one"), and the gap pre-exists in the committed view, so it is not a suggestion-6 deviation. No truthfulness or incentive claim is affected; nit severity is correct.

confirmed.location: Evaluator tab: "Comprehension Check Questions (must pass all):" and "Fielded-study opening:"
confirmed.claim: These two research-team labels are not in square brackets, so under the doc's own convention they read as verbatim participant-facing text; the doc also never specifies what happens on a failed check. [sources: comprehension]
confirmed.why: Risk of the labels (or the unexplained "must pass all" policy) leaking into the fielded survey.
confirmed.fix: Bracket both labels and add a bracketed note stating the fail policy (e.g., "[screen-out on any wrong answer; participants may review instructions first]").
confirmed.verify_note: Both labels appear unbracketed in both views (accepted/committed lines 96 and 119), and "Fielded-study opening:" shares a line with genuine participant text, so the convention violation is real; no bracketed design note anywhere specifies the CQ fail policy beyond "(must pass all)". Practical leak risk is low since many other structural labels (Consent, Instructions:, NEW/OLD, Proposed:) are also unbracketed and obviously headers, so nit is the correct severity.

confirmed.location: Endorser CQ intro "We want to ensure you understand how your earnings will be calculated"; evaluator CQ3 "affiliated with"; evaluator task paragraph "a subset of"
confirmed.claim: Small vocabulary mismatches: the CQ intro promises earnings questions but CQ2 is about task structure; "affiliated" (CQ3) is never used in the accepted instructions; "subset" is above target reading level. [sources: comprehension]
confirmed.why: None blocks a unique correct answer, but each adds friction for the average-reading-level participant.
confirmed.fix: Intro → "...you understand the study and how your earnings are calculated"; CQ3 keyed option → "The endorser's own organization (the one the endorser was assigned to)"; "subset" → "some".
confirmed.verify_note: All three quotes verified verbatim: the CQ intro (line 26, both views) promises earnings questions while endorser CQ2 asks about must-endorse structure; "affiliated" appears only in evaluator CQ3 (line 130), never in the accepted (or even committed) evaluator instructions; "a subset of" is in the accepted task paragraph (line 104, retained by suggestion 24). None blocks a unique correct answer or breaks truthfulness, so nit severity stands.

confirmed.location: Evaluator tab: "a stronger endorsement earns more if their candidate scores higher..." and "If their candidate wins, the more you wager..." vs. "correct if the endorsed candidate scored higher"
confirmed.claim: Tense is inconsistent with the realized state of the world: candidates' scores already exist when evaluators read this, and suggestion 31 correctly switched its sentence to past tense while suggestions 25 and 26 remain in present tense. [sources: mechanics, fidelity]
confirmed.why: Not a falsity, but mixed tense can make participants think outcomes are still to be generated, which matters for how they interpret outcome feedback; consistent past tense reinforces the (true) fact that outcomes are predetermined, preempting suspicion about "real-time" results.
